title: Τόξον καὶ ὀϊστός
about: Eurymachus says the suitors do not think Penelope will marry the stranger, but they dread the gossip that a wandering beggar strung the bow they could not. Penelope answers that men who devour a house have no good name to lose, and asks that the stranger be given the bow, promising him clothes, a javelin, a sword and sandals if he strings it. Telemachus takes the matter out of her hands: the bow is his to give, and she is to go back to her loom. She goes up, weeps for Odysseus, and sleeps. The suitors jeer at the swineherd carrying the bow, Telemachus threatens the swineherd, the suitors laugh the matter off, and Eumaeus puts it in Odysseus’ hands. Eurycleia shuts the doors of the hall at his word, and Philoetius makes the courtyard gates fast with a ship’s rope. While the suitors mutter, Odysseus turns the bow over, strings it as easily as a singer strings a lyre, and tries the string, which sings like a swallow. Zeus thunders. Odysseus shoots an arrow through the axes from his seat, tells Telemachus that the stranger has not shamed him and that it is time for supper and song, and nods; Telemachus arms himself and takes his stand beside his father.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτ’ Εὐρύμαχος, Πολύβου πάϊς, ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: Her then in turn spoke Eurymachus, Polybus’ son, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Eurymachus, son of Polybus, spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: τὴν is the pronoun ‘her’, Penelope, who finished speaking at the end of the previous part, and αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks the new speech as a reply. Εὐρύμαχος, Πολύβου πάϊς is a name with its patronymic, πάϊς being the epic form of παῖς ‘son’. ἀντίον ηὔδα ‘spoke face to face’ closes the line; ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’.

sentences.t:
κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρον Πηνελόπεια,
οὔ τί σε τόνδ’ ἄξεσθαι ὀϊόμεθ’·
sentences.l:
“Daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope,
not at all you this man to take-home we suppose;
sentences.i: “Daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope, we do not suppose that you will take this man home as your husband;
sentences.n: κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο has a genitive in -οιο (Attic Ἰκαρίου); περίφρον is the vocative of περίφρων, Penelope’s stock epithet. ὀϊόμεθ’ is ‘we suppose’, the first person plural of ὀΐομαι with the final α elided: Eurymachus speaks for all the suitors. οὔ τί σε … ἄξεσθαι is an accusative and infinitive, ‘that you will take this man’; ἄξεσθαι is the future middle of ἄγω, ‘lead home as one’s own’.

sentences.t: οὐδὲ ἔοικεν·
sentences.l: nor is it fitting;
sentences.i: nor is it fitting;
sentences.n: οὐδὲ ἔοικεν is ‘nor is it fitting’. ἔοικεν is a perfect with present sense, ‘it is fitting, it suits’, and Eurymachus is echoing Penelope’s own closing words in the previous part, where she said that it was not fitting at all for the suitors to sit grieving at their feast over her possible marriage.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αἰσχυνόμενοι φάτιν ἀνδρῶν ἠδὲ γυναικῶν,
μή ποτέ τις εἴπῃσι κακώτερος ἄλλος Ἀχαιῶν
ἦ πολὺ χείρονες ἄνδρες ἀμύμονος ἀνδρὸς ἄκοιτιν
μνῶνται, οὐδέ τι τόξον ἐΰξοον ἐντανύουσιν·
sentences.l:
But feeling-shame at the talk of men and of women,
lest ever someone should say, a baser other of the Achaeans:
‘Truly, far worse men a blameless man’s wife
woo, and not at all the well-polished bow do they string;
sentences.i: But we are ashamed before the talk of men and women, in case some other man, a baser one of the Achaeans, should say: ‘Men far worse are wooing the wife of a blameless man, and cannot string the well-polished bow;
sentences.n: αἰσχυνόμενοι ‘feeling shame’ takes the accusative φάτιν ‘talk, report’. μή ποτέ τις εἴπῃσι is a clause of fear, μή with the subjunctive (εἴπῃσι has the ending -σι(ν)): ‘lest anyone say’. What the imagined speaker says begins at ἦ ‘truly’ and runs to line 328; it is marked with single quotation marks. κακώτερος is the comparative of κακός, ‘baser’. ἀμύμονος is the stock ‘blameless’, whose true meaning is not known. ἐντανύουσιν is ‘they string’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄλλος τις πτωχὸς ἀνὴρ ἀλαλήμενος ἐλθὼν
ῥηϊδίως ἐτάνυσσε βιόν, διὰ δ’ ἧκε σιδήρου.
sentences.l:
but some other beggar, a man wandering, having come,
easily strung the bow, and shot through the iron.’
sentences.i: but some other beggar, a wanderer who has come, strung the bow with ease and shot through the iron.’
sentences.n: The supposed gossip goes on. ἀλαλήμενος, the perfect participle of ἀλάομαι, is ‘wandering’. ἐτάνυσσε is the aorist of τανύω ‘stretch’, which of a bow means ‘string’; βιόν is the accusative of βιός ‘bow’, a poetic word that differs from βίος ‘life’ only in its accent. διὰ δ’ ἧκε is tmesis for διῆκε ‘shot through’, with the genitive σιδήρου ‘the iron’, the axe-heads. The single quotation closes here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐρέουσ’, ἡμῖν δ’ ἂν ἐλέγχεα ταῦτα γένοιτο.
sentences.l: Thus they will say, and to us would these reproaches become.”
sentences.i: That is what they will say, and it would become a disgrace to us.”
sentences.n: ὣς ἐρέουσ’ is ‘so they will say’: ἐρέουσι is the future of ἐρέω ‘say’, with its final ι elided. ἔλεγχος, plural ἐλέγχεα, is ‘reproach, disgrace’ and ἂν … γένοιτο is a potential optative, ‘would become’. The turn to ἡμῖν ‘to us’ is the point of the whole speech: what troubles the suitors is the shame. This ends Eurymachus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν is the pronoun ‘him’, Eurymachus; αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks a reply. προσέειπε is the aorist ‘addressed’, Homer’s form of προσεῖπε. περίφρων Πηνελόπεια is her stock name and epithet; περίφρων ‘circumspect’ is built on περί ‘around’ and φρήν ‘mind’. This is a different reply-formula from ἠμείβετο and ἀντίον ηὔδα, and the English keeps the three apart.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύμαχ’, οὔ πως ἔστιν ἐϋκλεῖας κατὰ δῆμον
ἔμμεναι οἳ δὴ οἶκον ἀτιμάζοντες ἔδουσιν
ἀνδρὸς ἀριστῆος·
sentences.i: “Eurymachus, there is no way that men of good name in the land can be those who dishonour and devour the house of a man among the best;
sentences.n: Εὐρύμαχ’ is a vocative with its final α elided. οὔ πως ἔστιν ‘there is in no way’ takes an accusative and infinitive: ἐϋκλεῖας is the accusative plural of ἐϋκλεής ‘of good fame’ and agrees with an unstated ‘those men’, the antecedent of οἳ δὴ … ἔδουσιν ‘who indeed devour’ (ἔδουσιν is from ἔδω, the poetic ‘eat’, Attic ἐσθίω). ἔμμεναι is the epic ‘be’. ἀριστῆος is the genitive of ἀριστεύς ‘best man’. The man is Odysseus, though the line does not name him.

sentences.t: τί δ’ ἐλέγχεα ταῦτα τίθεσθε;
sentences.l: but why these reproaches do you make?
sentences.i: Why, then, do you count these things a disgrace?
sentences.n: τίθεσθε is the middle of τίθημι, ‘put for yourselves, count as’, so the question is ‘why do you make these things reproaches?’ ἐλέγχεα ταῦτα repeats Eurymachus’ own words from line 329 and turns them back on him: men who live off another man’s house have no standing to fear disgrace.

sentences.t:
οὗτος δὲ ξεῖνος μάλα μὲν μέγας ἠδ’ εὐπηγής,
πατρὸς δ’ ἐξ ἀγαθοῦ γένος εὔχεται ἔμμεναι υἱός.
sentences.l:
But this stranger is very tall and well-built,
and from a good father in lineage he claims to be a son.
sentences.i: This stranger, for his part, is very tall and well built, and claims to be, by birth, the son of a good father.
sentences.n: οὗτος is ‘this’, pointing to the stranger. μάλα μὲν μέγας ἠδ’ εὐπηγής is ‘very tall and well-built’; εὐπηγής is built on πήγνυμι ‘fix, join’ and means well put together. πατρὸς δ’ ἐξ ἀγαθοῦ is ‘from a good father’, with ἐξ and the genitive, and γένος is an accusative of respect, ‘in lineage’. εὔχεται ἔμμεναι υἱός ‘claims to be a son’ takes the nominative υἱός as predicate.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε οἱ δότε τόξον ἐΰξοον, ὄφρα ἴδωμεν.
sentences.l: But come, give him the well-polished bow, so that we may see.
sentences.i: So come, give him the well-polished bow, and let us see.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, introducing a command. οἱ is the dative pronoun ‘to him’, the stranger; δότε is the plural imperative of δίδωμι, addressed to the suitors. ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive ἴδωμεν gives purpose: ‘so that we may see’. ἐΰξοον ‘well-polished’ is the stock adjective of the bow and comes from ξέω ‘plane, polish’.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἐξερέω, τὸ δὲ καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.l: For thus I will declare, and this too fulfilled shall be;
sentences.i: For I will say it in this way, and what I say will also be fulfilled:
sentences.n: ὧδε ‘thus’ looks ahead to the promise that follows. ἐξερέω is the uncontracted future ‘I will speak out, declare’. τὸ is the pronoun ‘this’, and τετελεσμένον ἔσται, the perfect passive participle of τελέω with the future of εἰμί, is ‘will be accomplished’: Penelope pledges herself to carry the promise out.

sentences.t:
εἴ κέ μιν ἐντανύσῃ, δώῃ δέ οἱ εὖχος Ἀπόλλων,
ἕσσω μιν χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε, εἵματα καλά,
δώσω δ’ ὀξὺν ἄκοντα, κυνῶν ἀλκτῆρα καὶ ἀνδρῶν,
καὶ ξίφος ἄμφηκες·
sentences.l:
If he strings it, and Apollo grants him glory,
I will clothe him in a cloak and a tunic, fine clothes,
and I will give a sharp javelin, a warder-off of dogs and of men,
and a double-edged sword;
sentences.i: If he strings it, and Apollo grants him glory, I will clothe him in a cloak and a tunic, fine clothes, and give him a sharp javelin, a defence against dogs and men, and a double-edged sword;
sentences.n: εἴ κέ … ἐντανύσῃ opens a future condition with the subjunctive (κε = ἄν). The first μιν is the bow; the second, with ἕσσω, is the stranger, and οἱ is also ‘to him’. δώῃ is the aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι, εὖχος is ‘glory, triumph’, and ἕσσω is the future of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’. The gifts are a cloak and tunic, a javelin ‘that wards off dogs and men’ (ἀλκτῆρα), and a sword.

sentences.t:
δώσω δ’ ὑπὸ ποσσὶ πέδιλα,
πέμψω δ’ ὅππη μιν κραδίη θυμός τε κελεύει.
sentences.l:
and I will give sandals under his feet,
and I will send him where heart and spirit bid him.”
sentences.i: I will give him sandals for his feet, and send him wherever his heart and spirit bid him.”
sentences.n: ὑπὸ ποσσὶ is ‘under his feet’, the dative plural of πούς, which is where sandals are worn. ὅππη is the Homeric form of ὅπῃ ‘where’, so πέμψω … ὅππη μιν … κελεύει is ‘I will send him wherever his heart and spirit bid’. This repeats, with changes, a gift-list used earlier in the poem, and it ends Penelope’s speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘her’, Penelope; αὖ ‘in turn’ marks the reply. πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is Telemachus’ stock epithet, the perfect participle of a verb meaning ‘be wise’. ἀντίον ηὔδα ‘spoke face to face’ is the same ending as in line 320. Telemachus now speaks to his mother as master of the house.

sentences.t:
μῆτερ ἐμή, τόξον μὲν Ἀχαιῶν οὔ τις ἐμεῖο
κρείσσων, ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλω, δόμεναί τε καὶ ἀρνήσασθαι,
οὔθ’ ὅσσοι κραναὴν Ἰθάκην κάτα κοιρανέουσιν,
οὔθ’ ὅσσοι νήσοισι πρὸς Ἤλιδος ἱπποβότοιο·
sentences.l:
“Mother mine, the bow, of the Achaeans no one than I
is mightier, to whom I wish, to give and to refuse,
neither as many as rocky Ithaca throughout play the lord,
nor as many as on the islands toward horse-pasturing Elis;
sentences.i: “My mother, of all the Achaeans no one has more power than I to give the bow or refuse it, to whomever I wish, neither those who lord it throughout rocky Ithaca, nor those on the islands toward horse-pasturing Elis;
sentences.n: μῆτερ ἐμή is ‘my mother’. τόξον μὲν is the topic, ‘as for the bow’. οὔ τις … κρείσσων is ‘no one is mightier’, with ἐμεῖο, a genitive of comparison (Attic ἐμοῦ). ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλω is ‘to whomever I wish’, and δόμεναι (= δοῦναι) and ἀρνήσασθαι are ‘to give’ and ‘to refuse’. οὔθ’ ὅσσοι … οὔθ’ ὅσσοι ‘neither as many as … nor as many as’ covers every lord of Ithaca and of the islands. κάτα is κατά placed after its noun.

sentences.t:
τῶν οὔ τίς μ’ ἀέκοντα βιήσεται, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλωμι
καὶ καθάπαξ ξείνῳ δόμεναι τάδε τόξα φέρεσθαι.
sentences.l:
Of these no one against my will will force me, if I wish
even outright to give to the stranger this bow to carry off.
sentences.i: None of them will force me against my will, if I choose to give the stranger this bow outright, to carry away.
sentences.n: τῶν is partitive, ‘of these’, and βιήσεται is the future of βιάομαι ‘use force on’; ἀέκοντα (= ἄκοντα) ‘unwilling’ agrees with μ’. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλωμι is ‘if I should wish’ (αἴ = εἰ, with κε and the subjunctive). καθάπαξ means ‘once for all, outright’. τάδε τόξα is plural in form, but one bow is meant, as often with τόξα; φέρεσθαι, the middle infinitive, is ‘to carry off for himself’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰς οἶκον ἰοῦσα τὰ σ’ αὐτῆς ἔργα κόμιζε,
ἱστόν τ’ ἠλακάτην τε, καὶ ἀμφιπόλοισι κέλευε
ἔργον ἐποίχεσθαι·
sentences.i: Go instead into the house and attend to your own work, the loom and the distaff, and tell your handmaids to get on with their tasks;
sentences.n: ἰοῦσα is the feminine participle of εἶμι ‘go’, and τὰ σ’ αὐτῆς ἔργα is ‘your own tasks’, with σ’ for σά. ἱστόν τ’ ἠλακάτην τε, the loom and the distaff, are in apposition to the tasks, the work of spinning and weaving. κέλευε is the imperative ‘bid’. ἀμφιπόλοισι is a dative plural in -οισι, ‘attendants’; ἐποίχεσθαι is ‘to go about, ply’. Telemachus sends his mother away from the men’s business.

sentences.t:
τόξον δ’ ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει
πᾶσι, μάλιστα δ’ ἐμοί·
sentences.l:
but the bow to men will be a care,
to all, and most of all to me;
sentences.i: As for the bow, it will be the concern of the men, of all of them, and most of all of me;
sentences.n: μελήσει is the future of μέλω ‘be a care to’, with the dative ἄνδρεσσι πᾶσι ‘for all men’; ἄνδρεσσι has the Homeric dative ending -εσσι. μάλιστα δ’ ἐμοί ‘and most of all for me’ leaves the verb to be understood. Telemachus treats the bow as a matter for the men of the house.

sentences.t: τοῦ γὰρ κράτος ἔστ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ.
sentences.l: for the mastery is mine within the house.”
sentences.i: for the authority in this house is mine.”
sentences.n: τοῦ points back to the speaker: ‘of him’, so that the clause says ‘the mastery within the house is mine’. κράτος is ‘power, mastery’; ἔστ’ is ἔστι with its ι elided, and ἐνί is ἐν. οἴκῳ is the house. These words end Telemachus’ speech.

sentences.t: ἡ μὲν θαμβήσασα πάλιν οἶκόνδε βεβήκει·
sentences.l: She, then, astonished, had gone back again homeward;
sentences.i: Astonished, she went back again to her chamber;
sentences.n: ἡ μέν ‘she’ is Penelope; the article is a pronoun in Homer. θαμβήσασα is the aorist participle of θαμβέω ‘be amazed’. βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had gone’, with the sense of a simple past, ‘went’. οἶκόνδε has the suffix -δε of motion towards: ‘homeward, to the house’.

sentences.t: παιδὸς γὰρ μῦθον πεπνυμένον ἔνθετο θυμῷ.
sentences.l: for her son’s prudent speech she laid to heart.
sentences.i: for she took to heart her son’s prudent words.
sentences.n: παιδός depends on μῦθον, ‘her son’s speech’. πεπνυμένον ‘prudent’ is Telemachus’ epithet moved to his words. ἔνθετο is the aorist middle of ἐντίθημι ‘put in’, and ἔνθετο θυμῷ is ‘laid to heart’. γάρ gives the reason for her astonishment and her retreat.

sentences.t:
ἐς δ’ ὑπερῷ’ ἀναβᾶσα σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξὶ
κλαῖεν ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆα, φίλον πόσιν, ὄφρα οἱ ὕπνον
ἡδὺν ἐπὶ βλεφάροισι βάλε γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l:
And up to the upper chamber having gone, with her attendant women,
she wept then for Odysseus, her dear husband, until upon her sleep,
sweet, upon her eyelids cast gleaming-eyed Athena.
sentences.i: She went up to her upper room with her attendant women and wept then for Odysseus, her dear husband, until gleaming-eyed Athena cast sweet sleep upon her eyelids.
sentences.n: ὑπερῷα are the upper rooms of the house; ἀναβᾶσα is the aorist participle of ἀναβαίνω ‘go up’. σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξί is ‘with attendant women’. κλαῖεν is the imperfect ‘wept’; Ὀδυσῆα is the accusative of the person wept for. ὄφρα ‘until’ takes the aorist βάλε ‘cast’, whose subject is γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη, ‘gleaming-eyed Athena’; ἡδύν ‘sweet’ stands at the start of the next line, apart from ὕπνον ‘sleep’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὁ τόξα λαβὼν φέρε καμπύλα δῖος ὑφορβός·
sentences.l: But he, having taken the bow, carried it, the bent one, the heavenly swineherd;
sentences.i: The heavenly swineherd, meanwhile, took up the bent bow and went carrying it;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but, and then’ turns to the swineherd; ὁ is the pronoun ‘he’. τόξα … καμπύλα is plural in form, but one bow is meant, and καμπύλα is ‘bent’. φέρε is the unaugmented imperfect ‘was carrying’. δῖος ὑφορβός is ‘the heavenly swineherd’: ὑφορβός is a second word for the swineherd Eumaeus, named συβώτης in line 362.

sentences.t: μνηστῆρες δ’ ἄρα πάντες ὁμόκλεον ἐν μεγάροισιν·
sentences.l: and the suitors all then shouted in the halls;
sentences.i: and all the suitors shouted in the halls;
sentences.n: ὁμόκλεον is the imperfect of ὁμοκλέω ‘shout, call out’, often in rebuke or threat; the Greek does not say at whom, but the next speech shows it is at the swineherd and his burden. μνηστῆρες δ’ ἄρα πάντες is ‘and the suitors, all of them’. ἐν μεγάροισιν ‘in the halls’ has a dative plural in -οισιν.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκε νέων ὑπερηνορεόντων·
sentences.l: Thus would someone say, of the overweening young men:
sentences.i: and one of the overbearing young men would say something like this:
sentences.n: ὧδε ‘thus’ announces a speech. εἴπεσκε is an iterative past in -σκ-, ‘used to say, would say’: no single voice but a kind of taunt. τις νέων ὑπερηνορεόντων is ‘one of the young men who are overbearing’; ὑπερηνορεόντων is a participle, ‘being over-bold’, and the phrase returns at line 401.

sentences.t:
πῆ δὴ καμπύλα τόξα φέρεις, ἀμέγαρτε συβῶτα,
πλαγκτέ;
sentences.l:
“Where indeed the bent bow are you carrying, unenviable swineherd,
straying one?
sentences.i: “Where on earth are you carrying the bent bow, luckless swineherd, you roamer?
sentences.n: πῆ δὴ is ‘where on earth’. ἀμέγαρτε is the vocative of ἀμέγαρτος, a word of abuse whose sense is uncertain; ‘not to be envied’, hence ‘luckless’, is the traditional guess. συβῶτα is the vocative of συβώτης ‘swineherd’. πλαγκτέ is the vocative of πλαγκτός ‘wandering, straying’, from πλάζω, here a jeer at a man who lives away from the town.

sentences.t:
τάχ’ αὖ σ’ ἐφ’ ὕεσσι κύνες ταχέες κατέδονται
οἶον ἀπ’ ἀνθρώπων, οὓς ἔτρεφες, εἴ κεν Ἀπόλλων
ἡμῖν ἱλήκῃσι καὶ ἀθάνατοι θεοὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.l:
Soon, in turn, upon you among the swine swift dogs will devour,
alone, away from men, whom you reared, if Apollo
to us be gracious, and the immortal gods other.”
sentences.i: Soon the swift dogs you reared will devour you among the swine, alone, away from men, if Apollo and the other immortal gods are gracious to us.”
sentences.n: τάχ’ αὖ is ‘soon, in turn’. ἐφ’ ὕεσσι is ‘among the swine’, a dative plural of ὗς in -εσσι. κατέδονται is the future of κατεσθίω ‘eat up’, with κύνες ταχέες ‘swift dogs’ as subject; οὓς ἔτρεφες ‘whom you reared’ points back to the dogs, and οἶον ἀπ’ ἀνθρώπων is ‘alone, away from men’. εἴ κεν … ἱλήκῃσι is ‘if … is gracious’, a subjunctive in -σι(ν): the threat is a curse that holds only if the gods favour the suitors.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάσαν, αὐτὰρ, ὁ θῆκε φέρων αὐτῇ ἐνὶ χώρῃ,
δείσας, οὕνεκα πολλοὶ ὁμόκλεον ἐν μεγάροισιν.
sentences.l:
So they spoke, but he set down, carrying it, in that very place,
fearing, because many were shouting in the halls.
sentences.i: So they spoke; but he set down what he was carrying in that very spot, frightened, because many were shouting in the halls.
sentences.n: φάσαν is the third plural imperfect of φημί without the augment, ‘they said’. The comma after αὐτάρ sets off ὁ, the swineherd. θῆκε φέρων is ‘set down what he was carrying’, and αὐτῇ ἐνὶ χώρῃ ‘in the very place’ has the intensive αὐτῇ. δείσας is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’; οὕνεκα is ‘because’. ὁμόκλεον repeats line 360.

sentences.t: Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἀπειλήσας ἐγεγώνει·
sentences.l: but Telemachus from the other side, having threatened, called aloud:
sentences.i: Telemachus, for his part, called out threateningly from the other side:
sentences.n: ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’ has the suffix -θεν ‘from’. ἀπειλήσας is the aorist participle of ἀπειλέω ‘threaten’, and ἐγεγώνει is the imperfect of γεγωνέω ‘call aloud’. The Greek does not say which side he stands on; his speech overrules the suitors’ taunts and is addressed to the swineherd.

sentences.t: ἄττα, πρόσω φέρε τόξα·
sentences.l: “Father, onward bring the bow;
sentences.i: “Father, bring the bow forward;
sentences.n: ἄττα is the respectful address of a younger man to an older one, ‘father’, with no tie of kinship; Telemachus uses it to the swineherd. φέρε is the imperative ‘bring’, πρόσω ‘forward, onward’, and τόξα is plural in form, one bow in sense.

sentences.t:
τάχ’ οὐκ εὖ πᾶσι πιθήσεις
μή σε καὶ ὁπλότερός περ ἐὼν ἀγρόνδε δίωμαι,
βάλλων χερμαδίοισι·
sentences.i: Soon you will not do well to obey everyone, lest I, though the younger, chase you off to the fields, pelting you with stones;
sentences.n: τάχ’ οὐκ εὖ πᾶσι πιθήσεις is ‘soon you will not do well to obey everyone’; πιθήσεις is the future of πείθομαι ‘obey’, with the dative πᾶσι. μή with the subjunctive δίωμαι is a warning, ‘lest I chase’. ὁπλότερός περ ἐὼν ‘though being younger’ has concessive περ. ἀγρόνδε is ‘to the field’ (-δε); χερμαδίοισι is a dative plural ‘with stones’, in -οισι.

sentences.t: βίηφι δὲ φέρτερός εἰμι.
sentences.l: for in strength stronger I am.
sentences.i: for in strength I am the stronger.
sentences.n: βίηφι is ‘by strength’, with the old ending -φι, here an instrumental dative. φέρτερος is ‘stronger’, a comparative; the δέ gives the reason for the threat in the line before.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ πάντων τόσσον, ὅσοι κατὰ δώματ’ ἔασι,
μνηστήρων χερσίν τε βίηφί τε φέρτερος εἴην·
sentences.l:
Would that so much than all, as many as throughout the halls are,
of the suitors, in hands and in strength stronger I were;
sentences.i: If only I were so much stronger in hands and strength than all of the suitors who are in the halls;
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ introduces a wish, ‘would that’, and φέρτερος εἴην is the optative of wish, ‘I were stronger’. πάντων … μνηστήρων is a genitive of comparison, ‘than all the suitors’, with ὅσοι κατὰ δώματ’ ἔασι ‘as many as are in the halls’ (ἔασι = εἰσί); τόσσον ‘so much’ goes with the comparative. χερσίν τε βίηφί τε is ‘in hands and in strength’, datives of respect.

sentences.t:
τῷ κε τάχα στυγερῶς τιν’ ἐγὼ πέμψαιμι νέεσθαι
ἡμετέρου ἐξ οἴκου, ἐπεὶ κακὰ μηχανόωνται.
sentences.l:
Then I would soon send hatefully some one to go
from our house, since evils they contrive.”
sentences.i: Then I would quickly send one of them off in misery from our house, since they are contriving evil.”
sentences.n: τῷ κε begins the conclusion, ‘then’, with κε and the optative πέμψαιμι ‘I would send’. τιν’ is ‘someone’. στυγερῶς is ‘hatefully’, so as to be painful to the man sent. νέεσθαι, the epic form of νεῖσθαι, is ‘to go’. κακὰ μηχανόωνται is ‘they contrive evils’, with the uncontracted form of μηχανάομαι. This ends Telemachus’ speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ἡδὺ γέλασσαν
μνηστῆρες, καὶ δὴ μέθιεν χαλεποῖο χόλοιο
Τηλεμάχῳ·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the suitors all laughed pleasantly at him, and they let go of their harsh anger against Telemachus;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’: ἔφαθ’ is the imperfect ἔφατο with its vowel elided. ἐπ’ αὐτῷ is ‘at him’. γέλασσαν is the aorist of γελάω ‘laugh’ without the augment. μέθιεν is the imperfect of μεθίημι ‘let go’ and takes the genitive χαλεποῖο χόλοιο ‘of harsh anger’; καὶ δή is ‘and so indeed’. The laughter relaxes the tension in the hall.

sentences.t:
τὰ δὲ τόξα φέρων ἀνὰ δῶμα συβώτης
ἐν χείρεσσ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ δαΐφρονι θῆκε παραστάς.
sentences.l:
and the bow, carrying it through the house, the swineherd
into the hands of Odysseus, wise-minded, placed, standing beside him.
sentences.i: and the swineherd, carrying the bow through the house, placed it in the hands of wise-hearted Odysseus, standing beside him.
sentences.n: τὰ … τόξα is ‘the bow’ (one bow, plural form), and τά here is the article as a demonstrative. φέρων ἀνὰ δῶμα is ‘carrying through the house’. ἐν χείρεσσ’ is a dative plural in -εσσι. δαΐφρων is of disputed meaning: ‘wise-minded’, from δαῆναι ‘learn’, or ‘war-minded’, from δαΐ ‘in battle’; the translation follows the first. παραστάς is the aorist participle of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’.

sentences.t: ἐκ δὲ καλεσσάμενος προσέφη τροφὸν Εὐρύκλειαν·
sentences.l: and, calling her out, addressed the nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: and he called the nurse Eurycleia out and said to her:
sentences.n: ἐκ … καλεσσάμενος is tmesis for ἐκκαλεσσάμενος, the aorist middle participle of ἐκκαλέω ‘call out’, with doubled σ. προσέφη ‘addressed’ takes the accusative τροφὸν Εὐρύκλειαν, ‘the nurse Eurycleia’. The subject is the swineherd, who has just put the bow in Odysseus’ hands.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος κέλεταί σε, περίφρων Εὐρύκλεια,
κληῗσαι μεγάροιο θύρας πυκινῶς ἀραρυίας.
sentences.l:
“Telemachus bids you, circumspect Eurycleia,
to lock the doors of the hall, tightly fitted.
sentences.i: “Telemachus bids you, circumspect Eurycleia, to lock the tight-fitting doors of the hall.
sentences.n: Eumaeus gives the order in Telemachus’ name. κέλεταί σε is ‘bids you’, κέλομαι taking an accusative and infinitive. περίφρων Εὐρύκλεια ‘circumspect Eurycleia’ gives the nurse the epithet used of Penelope. κληῗσαι is the aorist infinitive of κληΐω ‘lock’, and πυκινῶς ἀραρυίας, the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω, is ‘fitted tightly’, agreeing with θύρας.

sentences.t:
ἢν δέ τις ἢ στοναχῆς ἠὲ κτύπου ἔνδον ἀκούσῃ
ἀνδρῶν ἡμετέροισιν ἐν ἕρκεσι,
sentences.l:
and if anyone either of groaning or of din within hears
of men in our courts,
sentences.i: and if any of them hears groaning or the din of men inside our courts,
sentences.n: ἢν is ἐάν, so ἢν … ἀκούσῃ is ‘and if anyone hears’, with the aorist subjunctive; the verb of hearing takes the genitives στοναχῆς ἠὲ κτύπου ‘groaning or din’, and ἀνδρῶν ‘of men’ depends on both. ἡμετέροισιν ἐν ἕρκεσι is ‘in our courts’, ἕρκος being an enclosure, with a dative in -οισιν. The condition ends at the comma and the order itself follows in the next unit. Eumaeus repeats, in Telemachus’ name, the order Odysseus gave him in the previous part.

sentences.t:
μή τι θύραζε
προβλώσκειν, ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ ἀκὴν ἔμεναι παρὰ ἔργῳ.
sentences.l:
not at all out of doors
to go forth, but there in silence to stay beside their work.”
sentences.i: they are not to go out of doors at all, but to stay where they are, in silence, at their work.”
sentences.n: μή τι θύραζε προβλώσκειν is an infinitive standing for a command, ‘not to go out at all’, and it continues the order that began with κέλεταί σε in line 381; ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ ἀκὴν ἔμεναι is ‘but to stay there in silence’, ἔμεναι being the epic infinitive of εἰμί. θύραζε ‘out of doors’, αὐτοῦ ‘on the spot’ and ἀκήν ‘in silence’ are adverbs, and παρὰ ἔργῳ is ‘at their work’. These words end Eumaeus’ speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν, τῇ δ’ ἄπτερος ἔπλετο μῦθος,
κλήϊσεν δὲ θύρας μεγάρων εὖ ναιεταόντων.
sentences.l:
So then he spoke, and to her wingless was the speech,
and she shut the doors of the well-inhabited halls.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and for her the speech was wingless; she shut the doors of the well-inhabited halls.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν is ‘so he spoke out’. τῇ δ’ ἄπτερος ἔπλετο μῦθος ‘for her the speech was wingless’ turns the formula ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ inside out; it may mean that she made no reply, but the Greek does not say so. κλήϊσεν is the aorist of κληΐω ‘shut’ without the augment, now with Eurycleia as subject; εὖ ναιεταόντων is ‘well-inhabited’.

sentences.t:
σιγῇ δ’ ἐξ οἴκοιο Φιλοίτιος ἆλτο θύραζε,
κλήϊσεν δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα θύρας εὐερκέος αὐλῆς.
sentences.l:
In silence from the house Philoetius sprang outdoors,
and he shut then the doors of the well-fenced courtyard.
sentences.i: In silence Philoetius sprang out of the house, and then shut the doors of the well-secured courtyard.
sentences.n: σιγῇ is ‘in silence’. Φιλοίτιος is the cowherd, to whom Odysseus gave the task of locking the courtyard gates in the previous part. ἆλτο is an aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, and θύραζε ‘outdoors’ ends in -ζε, a variant of the direction suffix -δε. εὐερκέος is the genitive of εὐερκής ‘well-fenced’ (ἕρκος ‘fence’), agreeing with αὐλῆς.

sentences.t:
κεῖτο δ’ ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ ὅπλον νεὸς ἀμφιελίσσης
βύβλινον, ᾧ ῥ’ ἐπέδησε θύρας, ἐς δ’ ἤϊεν αὐτός·
sentences.l:
There lay beneath the portico a rope of a ship curved on both sides,
of papyrus, with which he bound the doors, and in he went himself;
sentences.i: Under the portico lay the papyrus rope of a ship curved on both sides; with it he made the doors fast, and then went in himself;
sentences.n: κεῖτο is ‘was lying’, from κεῖμαι. αἴθουσα is the roofed portico before the hall. ὅπλον is any piece of tackle, here a rope; νεὸς ἀμφιελίσσης is traditionally ‘of a ship curved on both sides’, and βύβλινον is ‘of papyrus’ (βύβλος). ᾧ ῥ’ ἐπέδησε is ‘with which he bound’, ᾧ the relative dative. ἤϊεν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘went’, and ἐς … ἤϊεν ‘went in’ shows ἐς as an adverb.

sentences.t:
ἕζετ’ ἔπειτ’ ἐπὶ δίφρον ἰών, ἔνθεν περ ἀνέστη,
εἰσορόων Ὀδυσῆα.
sentences.l:
He sat down then, going to the stool, from where he had risen,
looking at Odysseus.
sentences.i: Then he went to the stool he had risen from, and sat down, looking at Odysseus.
sentences.n: ἕζετ’ is ἕζετο, ‘sat down’. ἐπὶ δίφρον ἰών is ‘going to the stool’, and ἔνθεν περ ἀνέστη is ‘from the very place he had risen’, with intensive περ. εἰσορόων is the uncontracted participle of εἰσοράω ‘look at’. Philoetius takes his old seat so that he can watch Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἤδη τόξον ἐνώμα
πάντη ἀναστρωφῶν, πειρώμενος ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα,
μὴ κέρα ἶπες ἔδοιεν ἀποιχομένοιο ἄνακτος.
sentences.l:
But he now the bow was handling,
turning it about, testing it here and there,
lest the horn the worms might have eaten, with its lord gone away.
sentences.i: But Odysseus was already handling the bow, turning it over and testing it this way and that, in case worms had eaten the horn while its lord was away.
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ ‘but he’ is Odysseus. ἐνώμα is the imperfect of νωμάω ‘handle’, ἀναστρωφῶν the participle ‘turning about’, and πειρώμενος ‘testing’; ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα is ‘this way and that’. μὴ … ἔδοιεν is μή with the optative after a past tense, ‘in case they had eaten’. ἶπες are worms that eat horn, and κέρα is the bow’s horn. ἀποιχομένοιο ἄνακτος is a genitive absolute, ‘with its lord gone’.

sentences.t: ὧδε τις εἴπεσκεν ἰδὼν ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον·
sentences.l: Thus would someone say, looking at another near by:
sentences.i: and one of them, looking at the man next to him, would say something like this:
sentences.n: ὧδε τις εἴπεσκεν is ‘thus someone would say’, with the iterative past in -σκ-. ἰδὼν ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον is ‘looking toward another near by’: the suitors mutter to their neighbours, one pair after another.

sentences.t: ἦ τις θηητὴρ καὶ ἐπίκλοπος ἔπλετο τόξων·
sentences.l: “Truly, some admirer and thievish-one of bows he has become;
sentences.i: “Surely he is some admirer of bows, and a trickster;
sentences.n: ἦ τις θηητὴρ καὶ ἐπίκλοπος … τόξων is ‘truly some admirer and sly one of bows’; the genitive says what he admires. ἦ with the circumflex is ‘truly’. θηητήρ is built on θηέομαι ‘gaze at in wonder’, ἐπίκλοπος is ‘thievish, sly’, and ἔπλετο is the old aorist of πέλομαι ‘be, become’, used like a present.
sentences.mark: A suitor remarks on the stranger

sentences.t:
ἤ ῥά νύ που τοιαῦτα καὶ αὐτῷ οἴκοθι κεῖται
ἢ ὅ γ’ ἐφορμᾶται ποιησέμεν, ὡς ἐνὶ χερσὶ
νωμᾷ ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα κακῶν ἔμπαιος ἀλήτης.
sentences.l:
Either, I suppose, such things for himself also at home lie
or he is set on making them, the way in his hands
he turns it here and there, versed in evils, the vagrant.”
sentences.i: Either he has bows like this lying at home himself, or he is bent on making one, the way he turns it in his hands this way and that, this vagrant versed in wickedness.”
sentences.n: ἤ ῥά νύ που … ἢ is ‘either, I suppose, … or’, the first half a guess. τοιαῦτα ‘such things’ means bows like this one; αὐτῷ ‘for himself’; οἴκοθι ‘at home’ has the place suffix -θι. ἐφορμᾶται ποιησέμεν is ‘is set on making’, with the future infinitive. ὡς … νωμᾷ is ‘the way he handles’, and κακῶν ἔμπαιος ἀλήτης is ‘a vagrant versed in evils’, ἔμπαιος taking the genitive. This ends the speech.

sentences.t: ἄλλος δ’ αὖ εἴπεσκε νέων ὑπερηνορεόντων·
sentences.l: But another, in turn, would say, of the overweening young men:
sentences.i: But another of the overbearing young men would say in his turn:
sentences.n: ἄλλος δ’ αὖ ‘and another in turn’ opens a second taunt, with εἴπεσκε the iterative ‘would say’ as at line 361 and the same phrase νέων ὑπερηνορεόντων ‘of the overbearing young men’. The two speeches show the suitors passing their opinions round the hall.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ δὴ τοσσοῦτον ὀνήσιος ἀντιάσειεν
ὡς οὗτός ποτε τοῦτο δυνήσεται ἐντανύσασθαι.
sentences.l:
“Would that so much of profit he might meet
as this man will ever be able to string this.”
sentences.i: “If only he might meet with as much profit as this man will ever be able to string this bow!”
sentences.n: αἲ γὰρ δή is ‘if only, indeed’, a wish. ἀντιάσειεν is the optative of ἀντιάω ‘meet with, share in’, taking the genitive ὀνήσιος ‘of profit’; its subject is not named. τοσσοῦτον … ὡς is ‘just so much … as’: he wishes the man as much profit as he will ever have success in stringing the bow, that is none. δυνήσεται is the future of δύναμαι, ἐντανύσασθαι the aorist middle infinitive ‘to string’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν μνηστῆρες·
sentences.l: So then spoke the suitors;
sentences.i: So the suitors spoke;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν is ‘so they spoke’. ἔφαν is the third plural imperfect of φημί, as ἔφαθ’ at line 376 is the singular. The half-line closes the suitors’ talk before the poet turns back to Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς,
αὐτίκ’ ἐπεὶ μέγα τόξον ἐβάστασε καὶ ἴδε πάντη,
sentences.l:
but many-wiled Odysseus,
as soon as the great bow he had weighed in hand and looked over on every side,
sentences.i: but Odysseus of many wiles, as soon as he had lifted the great bow and looked it over on every side,
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’ turns to Odysseus, and πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’ is his stock epithet. The sentence is long and its main verb, τάνυσεν, does not arrive until line 409, after a comparison; the unit stops at a comma only for that reason. αὐτίκ’ ἐπεί is ‘as soon as’. ἐβάστασε is ‘lifted, weighed in the hand’; ἴδε is the unaugmented aorist ‘looked at’, and πάντη is ‘on every side’.

sentences.t:
ὡς ὅτ’ ἀνὴρ φόρμιγγος ἐπιστάμενος καὶ ἀοιδῆς
ῥηϊδίως ἐτάνυσσε νέῳ περὶ κόλλοπι χορδήν,
ἅψας ἀμφοτέρωθεν ἐϋστρεφὲς ἔντερον οἰός,
sentences.l:
as when a man, skilled in the lyre and in song,
easily stretches on a new peg a string,
fastening at both ends well-twisted gut of a sheep,
sentences.i: as when a man skilled in the lyre and in song easily stretches a string round a new peg, fastening at both ends the well-twisted gut of a sheep,
sentences.n: ὡς ὅτ’ ἀνήρ is ‘as when a man’, the opening of a comparison; ἐπιστάμενος ‘knowing, skilled’ takes the genitives φόρμιγγος καὶ ἀοιδῆς. ἐτάνυσσε is an aorist in a comparison, which English renders with a present. κόλλοψ is the peg round which a lyre string is wound; χορδή is ‘string’. ἅψας is ‘fastening’, ἀμφοτέρωθεν ‘at both ends’, ἐϋστρεφές ‘well-twisted’, and οἰός is the genitive of οἶς ‘sheep’. ῥηϊδίως ‘easily’ was used at line 328 of the beggar of the suitors’ fears.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἄτερ σπουδῆς τάνυσεν μέγα τόξον Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l: so then without effort he strung the great bow, Odysseus.
sentences.i: so, without effort, Odysseus strung the great bow.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ‘so’ answers ὡς ὅτ’ at line 406, and with it the sentence begun at line 404 reaches its verb. τάνυσεν is the aorist of τανύω, ‘strung’, picking up ἐτάνυσσε from the comparison. ἄτερ σπουδῆς is ‘without effort’; σπουδή is ‘haste, exertion’, and ἄτερ takes the genitive.

sentences.t: δεξιτερῇ ἄρα χειρὶ λαβὼν πειρήσατο νευρῆς·
sentences.l: In his right hand then, having taken it, he tried the string;
sentences.i: Taking it in his right hand, he tested the string;
sentences.n: δεξιτερῇ ἄρα χειρί is ‘in his right hand’, with δεξιτερός ‘right’ and the dative of instrument. λαβών is ‘having taken’ the bow. πειρήσατο, the aorist middle of πειράω ‘try’, takes the genitive νευρῆς ‘the string’, the part that sounds in the next line.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ὑπὸ καλὸν ἄεισε, χελιδόνι εἰκέλη αὐδήν.
sentences.l: and it beneath sang beautifully, like a swallow in voice.
sentences.i: and the string sang beautifully under his hand, like a swallow in its voice.
sentences.n: ἡ is the pronoun ‘it’, the string (νευρή is feminine). ὑπό is an adverb here, ‘beneath’; the Greek does not say beneath what, so the English supplies the touch. καλόν ‘beautifully’ is a neuter adjective used as an adverb. ἄεισε is the unaugmented aorist of ἀείδω ‘sing’, said of an instrument. χελιδόνι εἰκέλη αὐδήν is ‘like a swallow in voice’, εἰκέλη agreeing with ἡ and αὐδήν an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρσιν δ’ ἄρ’ ἄχος γένετο μέγα, πᾶσι δ’ ἄρα χρὼς
ἐτράπετο·
sentences.l:
On the suitors then grief came great, and on all the colour
turned;
sentences.i: Great grief came upon the suitors, and the colour of every one of them changed;
sentences.n: ἄχος μέγα is ‘great grief’, and γένετο is the unaugmented aorist ‘came to be’. χρώς is ‘skin, complexion’; πᾶσι δ’ ἄρα χρώς ἐτράπετο is ‘and the colour turned for all of them’, that is, they changed colour. ἐτράπετο is the aorist middle of τρέπω, the verb held over to the start of the next line.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς δὲ μεγάλ’ ἔκτυπε σήματα φαίνων·
sentences.l: and Zeus greatly thundered, signs showing;
sentences.i: and Zeus thundered loudly, showing signs;
sentences.n: μεγάλ’ is the neuter plural μεγάλα used as an adverb, ‘greatly’; ἔκτυπε is the aorist of κτυπέω ‘crash, thunder’. σήματα φαίνων is ‘showing signs’, and the thunder is the sign; the next line shows Odysseus reading it as a portent.

sentences.t: γήθησέν τ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l: and rejoiced then, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.i: And much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus was glad.
sentences.n: γήθησεν is the aorist of γηθέω ‘rejoice’, and τ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα ‘and then’ links his joy to the sign just given. πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς fills the end of the line: πολύτλας ‘much-enduring’ is built on πολύ and the root τλα- ‘endure’, and δῖος is ‘heavenly’.

sentences.t: ὅττι ῥά οἱ τέρας ἧκε Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω·
sentences.l: because to him a portent had sent the son of Cronus of crooked cunning;
sentences.i: because the son of Cronus of crooked cunning had sent him a portent;
sentences.n: ὅττι ‘because’ gives the reason for his joy; οἱ is ‘for him’, τέρας ‘portent, sign’, and ἧκε ‘sent’. Κρόνου πάϊς is Zeus, ‘son of Cronus’, with πάϊς the epic form of παῖς. ἀγκυλομήτεω is the genitive of ἀγκυλομήτης, which agrees with Κρόνου: ἀγκύλος means ‘curved, crooked’ and μῆτις ‘cunning’. The epithet is traditionally ‘of crooked counsel’, but its exact sense is uncertain.

sentences.t:
εἵλετο δ’ ὠκὺν ὀϊστόν, ὅ οἱ παρέκειτο τραπέζῃ
γυμνός·
sentences.l:
And he took a swift arrow, which beside him lay on the table,
bare;
sentences.i: He took a swift arrow, the one that lay bare on the table beside him;
sentences.n: εἵλετο is the aorist middle of αἱρέω ‘take’. ὠκὺν ὀϊστόν is ‘a swift arrow’. ὅ is the relative ‘which’, οἱ ‘by him’, and παρέκειτο is the imperfect of παράκειμαι ‘lie beside’, with the dative τραπέζῃ ‘on the table’. γυμνός ‘bare’ means out of the quiver, as the next lines say.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἄλλοι κοίλης ἔντοσθε φαρέτρης
κείατο, τῶν τάχ’ ἔμελλον Ἀχαιοὶ πειρήσεσθαι.
sentences.l:
but the others inside the hollow quiver
lay, of which soon were about the Achaeans to make trial.
sentences.i: while the others lay inside the hollow quiver, which the Achaeans were soon to try.
sentences.n: τοὶ δ’ ἄλλοι is ‘but the others’, τοί being the pronoun form. κοίλης ἔντοσθε φαρέτρης is ‘inside the hollow quiver’. κείατο is ‘were lying’, the imperfect of κεῖμαι with the epic ending -ατο. τῶν is ‘of which’; ἔμελλον with the future infinitive is ‘were about to’, and πειράομαι ‘make trial of’ takes the genitive.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥ’ ἐπὶ πήχει ἑλὼν ἕλκεν νευρὴν γλυφίδας τε,
αὐτόθεν ἐκ δίφροιο καθήμενος, ἧκε δ’ ὀϊστὸν
ἄντα τιτυσκόμενος,
sentences.i: He set it to the bow-grip and drew back the string and the notched end, sitting just where he was on the stool, and let fly the arrow, aiming straight ahead,
sentences.n: τόν is the arrow. ἐπὶ πήχει ἑλών: πῆχυς is ‘forearm’, and here it names some part of the bow, probably the grip; the exact sense is uncertain. γλυφίδες are the notches of the arrow’s end, where the string sits, so ἕλκεν νευρὴν γλυφίδας τε is ‘drew back the string and the notched end’. αὐτόθεν is ‘from that very spot’, ἐκ δίφροιο καθήμενος ‘sitting on the stool’. ἧκε is ‘let fly’; ἄντα τιτυσκόμενος is ‘aiming straight’. The unit stops at a comma because the sentence runs on.

sentences.t:
πελέκεων δ’ οὐκ ἤμβροτε πάντων
πρώτης στειλειῆς, διὰ δ’ ἀμπερὲς ἦλθε θύραζε
ἰὸς χαλκοβαρής·
sentences.i: and he did not miss the first haft-hole of all the axes, and the bronze-heavy arrow went right through and out of doors;
sentences.n: πελέκεων is the genitive plural of πέλεκυς ‘axe’. οὐκ ἤμβροτε is the aorist of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’ with the genitive πρώτης στειλειῆς, ‘the first haft-hole’: στειλειή is the hole in the axe-head that holds the haft. The phrasing is compressed: he does not miss the first, and the arrow goes διὰ … ἀμπερές ‘right through’ (tmesis) and θύραζε ‘out of doors’. ἰὸς χαλκοβαρής is ‘the bronze-heavy arrow’.

sentences.t: ὁ δὲ Τηλέμαχον προσέειπε·
sentences.l: and he addressed Telemachus:
sentences.i: and he spoke to Telemachus:
sentences.n: ὁ δὲ ‘and he’ is Odysseus. προσέειπε is the same aorist ‘addressed’ as in line 330, but here it takes the accusative Τηλέμαχον. There is no αὖτε ‘in turn’, because this speech does not answer anyone.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, οὔ σ’ ὁ ξεῖνος ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἐλέγχει
ἥμενος, οὐδέ τι τοῦ σκοποῦ ἤμβροτον οὐδέ τι τόξον
δὴν ἔκαμον τανύων·
sentences.i: “Telemachus, the stranger sitting in your halls brings no shame on you; I did not miss the mark in any way, nor did I toil long to string the bow;
sentences.n: ἐλέγχει is ‘puts to shame, disgraces’, from ἐλέγχω, with σε as object; Odysseus speaks of ‘the stranger’ first, then of himself. οὐδέ τι … οὐδέ τι is ‘nor at all … nor at all’. ἥμενος is ‘sitting’. τοῦ σκοποῦ is a genitive after ἤμβροτον ‘I missed’, ‘the mark’. δὴν ἔκαμον τανύων is ‘I toiled long stringing’, κάμνω taking a participle, and δήν ‘for long’.

sentences.t:
ἔτι μοι μένος ἔμπεδόν ἐστιν,
οὐχ ὥς με μνηστῆρες ἀτιμάζοντες ὄνονται.
sentences.l:
Still to me strength is firm,
not as me the suitors, dishonouring, scorn.
sentences.i: My strength is still firm, not as the suitors scorn me, dishonouring me.
sentences.n: ἔτι μοι μένος ἔμπεδόν ἐστιν is ‘my strength is still firm’. οὐχ ὥς με … ὄνονται is ‘not as they scorn me’: ὄνονται is from ὄνομαι ‘find fault with, scorn’, and ἀτιμάζοντες ‘dishonouring’ goes with the suitors. It answers Odysseus’ own doubt in the previous part, whether wandering had destroyed his strength.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ὥρη καὶ δόρπον Ἀχαιοῖσιν τετυκέσθαι
ἐν φάει, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα καὶ ἄλλως ἑψιάασθαι
μολπῇ καὶ φόρμιγγι· τὰ γάρ τ’ ἀναθήματα δαιτός.
sentences.l:
But now it is time for supper too to be prepared for the Achaeans
in the light, and afterwards in other ways also to amuse ourselves
with song-and-dance and lyre; for these are the adornments of a feast.”
sentences.i: But now it is time for supper to be made ready for the Achaeans in daylight, and afterwards to amuse ourselves in other ways as well, with song and dance and the lyre; for these are the things that crown a feast.”
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ὥρη is ‘but now it is time’, followed by infinitives: δόρπον … τετυκέσθαι ‘for supper to be made ready’ and ἑψιάασθαι ‘to amuse ourselves’, uncontracted. ἐν φάει is ‘in the light’, while it is still day. ἄλλως ‘in other ways’ and καὶ ‘also’ point to the entertainment that follows the meal. μολπῇ καὶ φόρμιγγι are datives of means. In the last clause τά is ‘these’, song and lyre, and τε is the epic particle that marks a general truth; ἀναθήματα are things ‘set up’ or ‘added’, the adornments of a feast, with ‘are’ left out. With it Odysseus’ speech comes to an end.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι νεῦσεν·
sentences.l: He spoke, and with his brows he nodded;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and nodded with his brows;
sentences.n: ἦ καί is ‘he spoke, and’, ἦ being the old form ‘he said’. ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι νεῦσεν is ‘nodded with his brows’, a silent signal; the lines that follow show what Telemachus does in answer.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἀμφέθετο ξίφος ὀξὺ
Τηλέμαχος, φίλος υἱὸς Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο,
ἀμφὶ δὲ χεῖρα φίλην βάλεν ἔγχεϊ, ἄγχι δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτοῦ
πὰρ θρόνον ἑστήκει κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ.
sentences.l:
and he girded on his sharp sword,
Telemachus, the dear son of Odysseus, divine,
and around the spear his dear hand he cast, and close to him
beside the chair he stood, armed with the fire-faced bronze.
sentences.i: Then Telemachus, the dear son of divine Odysseus, girded on his sharp sword, put his hand about his spear, and stood close beside him, next to the chair, armed with bronze that has the look of fire.
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ ‘and he’ is named in the next line, Τηλέμαχος. ἀμφέθετο is the aorist middle of ἀμφιτίθημι ‘put around oneself’. ἀμφὶ δὲ χεῖρα φίλην βάλεν ἔγχεϊ is ‘he cast his hand about the spear’, that is, gripped it; φίλην ‘dear’ is used almost as ‘own’. ἄγχι … αὐτοῦ is ‘close to him’, Odysseus, and ἑστήκει, the pluperfect of ἵστημι, is ‘stood’. κεκορυθμένος, from κόρυς ‘helmet’, is ‘armed’; αἴθοπι ‘fire-faced’ is built like αἶθοψ οἶνος.
